problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

A line in the plane is called *sunny* if it is not parallel to any of the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis, and the line $x+y=0$.

Let $n\ge3$ be a given integer. Determine all nonnegative integers $k$ such that there exist $n$ distinct lines in the plane satisfying both the following:
*   for all positive integers $a$ and $b$ with $a+b\le n+1$, the point $(a,b)$ is on at least one of the lines; and
*   exactly $k$ of the lines are sunny.
solution:
### Summary  

**a. Verdict**  
I have obtained a complete solution.  
The admissible numbers of sunny lines are  

\[
\boxed{\;k\in\{0,1,3\}\;}
\]

for every integer \(n\ge 3\).

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Reduction to a right‑triangle.**  
   Replace the \(n-k\) non‑sunny lines by \(n-k\) distinct vertical lines
   \(x=1,\dots ,x=n-k\).  
   A vertical line covers *all* points of the set  

   \[
   S_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid a+b\le n+1\},
   \]

   and any other non‑sunny line (horizontal or of slope \(-1\)) can cover at most
   one point in each column, therefore the vertical choice is never worse.
   After removing those columns the uncovered points are exactly  

   \[
   T_k=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid x+y\le k+1\},
   \tag{1}
   \]

   a right‑angled integer triangle of side‑length \(k\).  
   Consequently the original problem is equivalent to:

   > **Problem (*)** – For a given non‑negative integer \(k\) decide whether the
   > set \(T_k\) can be covered by exactly \(k\) *distinct sunny* lines.

2. **Maximum number of points of \(T_k\) on one sunny line.**  
   Write a sunny line in the integer form  

   \[
   p x-q y=c ,\qquad \gcd(p,q)=1,\;q>0,\;p\neq0,\;p\neq -q .
   \tag{2}
   \]

   All integer points on the line are  

   \[
   (x,y)=(x_0+qt,\;y_0+pt),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,
   \tag{3}
   \]

   where \((x_0,y_0)\) is a particular solution of (2).  
   Their sums satisfy  

   \[
   x+y=(x_0+y_0)+(p+q)t .
   \tag{4}
   \]

   Because the line is sunny, \(p+q\neq0\); hence the sum changes by at
   least \(|p+q|\ge 1\) when \(t\) varies by one.

   In the triangle \(T_k\) we have \(2\le x+y\le k+1\).  
   From (4) the number of admissible integers \(t\) is therefore at most  

   \[
   \Bigl\lfloor\frac{k+1-2}{|p+q|}\Bigr\rfloor+1\le
   \Bigl\lfloor\frac{k-1}{2}\Bigr\rfloor+1=
   \Bigl\lfloor\frac{k+1}{2}\Bigr\rfloor .
   \tag{5}
   \]

   Moreover, if \(|p+q|=1\) then \(|q|\ge 2\) (otherwise the line would be
   horizontal or have slope \(-1\)), and the condition \(1\le x\le k\) forces
   at most \(\bigl\lfloor k/q\bigr\rfloor+1\le\bigl\lfloor(k+1)/2\bigr\rfloor\)
   points.  Hence for **every** sunny line  

   \[
   \boxed{\;|\,\text{line}\cap T_k\,|\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac{k+1}{2}\Bigr\rfloor\;}
   \tag{6}
   \]

   and the bound is attained (see §5).

3. **Counting argument.**  
   The triangle \(T_k\) contains  

   \[
   |T_k|=\frac{k(k+1)}2
   \tag{7}
   \]

   points.  If we have exactly \(k\) sunny lines, (6) gives  

   \[
   k\Bigl\lfloor\frac{k+1}{2}\Bigr\rfloor\ge |T_k|
   =\frac{k(k+1)}2 .
   \tag{8}
   \]

   *If \(k\) is even*, write \(k=2m\).  Then the left–hand side of (8) equals
   \(2m\cdot m=m(2m)=k^{2}/2\), whereas the right–hand side equals
   \(m(2m+1)=k^{2}/2+m\).  Because \(m>0\), (8) is false.  
   Hence **no even \(k\ge2\) works**.

   *If \(k\) is odd*, write \(k=2m+1\).  Then
   \(\bigl\lfloor(k+1)/2\bigr\rfloor=m+1\) and (8) becomes an equality:

   \[
   (2m+1)(m+1)=\frac{(2m+1)(2m+2)}2 .
   \tag{9}
   \]

   Consequently every sunny line must contain **exactly**
   \(\bigl\lfloor(k+1)/2\bigr\rfloor=m+1\) points of \(T_k\), and the
   \(k\) lines must be pairwise disjoint.

4. **Sunny lines attaining the bound.**  
   Solving (2) with \(|p+q|=2\) gives three families of lines that contain
   \(m+1\) points of \(T_{2m+1}\):

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   L_{1}&: y = x ,\\
   L_{2}&: y = -2x + (2m+3),\\
   L_{3}&: y = -\tfrac12 x + \tfrac{2m+3}{2}.
   \end{aligned}
   \tag{10}
   \]

   Direct substitution shows

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   L_{1}&\cap T_{2m+1}= \{(i,i)\mid 1\le i\le m+1\},\\
   L_{2}&\cap T_{2m+1}= \{(i,2m+3-2i)\mid 1\le i\le m+1\},\\
   L_{3}&\cap T_{2m+1}= \{(2i-1,2m+4-2i)\mid 1\le i\le m+1\},
   \end{aligned}
   \]

   each set containing exactly \(m+1\) points, and the three sets are
   disjoint.  No other sunny line can contain \(m+1\) points of \(T_{2m+1}\)
   (otherwise \(|p+q|\) would be \(1\) and we would have the contradiction
   described in §2).  Hence **the only way to cover \(T_{2m+1}\) with
   \(2m+1\) sunny lines is to use the three lines (10) and no other sunny
   line**.  Consequently we must have \(2m+1\le 3\); i.e. \(k=1\) or
   \(k=3\).

5. **Putting the pieces together.**  

   *\(k=0\).*  
   Take the \(n\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n\).  All are non‑sunny and
   every point of \(S_n\) lies on the line with its \(x\)-coordinate.

   *\(k=1\).*  
   Use the \(n-1\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n-1\).  
   The only uncovered point is \((n,1)\).  Choose any sunny line through this
   point, e.g.  

   \[
   \ell:\; y=2x-2n+1 .
   \]

   The set of \(n\) lines (the \(n-1\) vertical ones and \(\ell\)) satisfies the
   requirements.

   *\(k=3\).*  
   Use the \(n-3\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n-3\).  
   The uncovered points are exactly the set \(T_3\):
   \[
   \{(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(2,2),(3,1)\}.
   \]
   The three sunny lines from (10) with \(m=1\),

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   L_{1}&: y=x,\\
   L_{2}&: y=-2x+5,\\
   L_{3}&: y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac52,
   \end{aligned}
   \]

   cover these six points point‑by‑point:

   \[
   \begin{array}{c|c}
   \text{point} & \text{line containing it}\\ \hline
   (1,1),(2,2) & L_{1}\\
   (1,3),(2,1) & L_{2}\\
   (1,2),(3,1) & L_{3}
   \end{array}
   \]

   Together with the vertical lines all points of \(S_n\) are covered.

   Thus for every \(n\ge3\) the values \(k=0,1,3\) are attainable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Detailed Solution  

Let  

\[
S_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid a+b\le n+1\},\qquad |S_n|=\frac{n(n+1)}2 .
\]

A line is **sunny** iff its slope is different from \(0,\infty,-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  Reduction to the triangle \(T_k\)

Assume we have a configuration of \(n\) distinct lines with exactly \(k\) sunny
lines.  Replace each non‑sunny line by a vertical line that passes through
the leftmost column not yet occupied by a vertical line.  A vertical line
covers **all** points of a column, whereas a horizontal line or a line of
slope \(-1\) can meet a column in at most one point.  Hence after the
replacement we still cover every point of \(S_n\) and we have exactly the same
number \(k\) of sunny lines.

Consequently we may (and shall) assume that the \(n-k\) non‑sunny lines are the
vertical lines  

\[
x=1,\;x=2,\dots ,x=n-k .
\tag{1.1}
\]

All points with abscissa \(a\le n-k\) are already covered.  The remaining
points are

\[
T_k=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid x+y\le k+1\},
\tag{1.2}
\]

a right‑angled integer triangle of side‑length \(k\).  Thus the original
problem is equivalent to **Problem (*)** stated in the summary.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  A bound for a sunny line inside \(T_k\)

Let a sunny line be given.  Multiplying its equation by a common denominator we
obtain an integer equation

\[
p x-q y=c ,\qquad \gcd(p,q)=1,\;q>0,\;p\neq0,\;p\neq -q .
\tag{2.1}
\]

All integer points on the line are described by (3) above:

\[
(x,y)=(x_0+qt,\;y_0+pt),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z .
\tag{2.2}
\]

Their sums satisfy (4):

\[
x+y=(x_0+y_0)+(p+q)t .
\tag{2.3}
\]

Because the line is sunny, \(p+q\neq0\); therefore the sum changes by at least
\(|p+q|\ge1\) when \(t\) varies by one.

Inside the triangle \(T_k\) we have \(2\le x+y\le k+1\).  From (2.3) the
number of admissible integers \(t\) is at most  

\[
\Bigl\lfloor\frac{k+1-2}{|p+q|}\Bigr\rfloor+1\le
\Bigl\lfloor\frac{k-1}{2}\Bigr\rfloor+1=
\Bigl\lfloor\frac{k+1}{2}\Bigr\rfloor .
\tag{2.4}
\]

If \(|p+q|=1\) then \(p+q=\pm1\).  The equality \(p+q=1\) forces
\(q\ge2\) (otherwise \(p=0\) which would give a horizontal line).  Because
\(x=x_0+qt\) must stay in the interval \([1,k]\), the number of admissible
\(t\) is at most \(\bigl\lfloor k/q\bigr\rfloor+1\le\bigl\lfloor(k+1)/2\bigr\rfloor\).
The same reasoning works for \(p+q=-1\).  Hence (2.4) holds for **every**
sunny line, and the bound is sharp (see §4).

\[
\boxed{|\,\text{sunny line}\cap T_k\,|\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac{k+1}{2}\Bigr\rfloor } .
\tag{2.5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  Counting argument

The triangle \(T_k\) contains  

\[
|T_k|=\frac{k(k+1)}2 .
\tag{3.1}
\]

If we have exactly \(k\) sunny lines, (2.5) yields  

\[
k\Bigl\lfloor\frac{k+1}{2}\Bigr\rfloor\ge\frac{k(k+1)}2 .
\tag{3.2}
\]

*Even \(k\).*  Write \(k=2m\;(m\ge1)\).  Then the left‑hand side of (3.2) equals
\(2m\cdot m=m(2m)=k^{2}/2\), whereas the right‑hand side equals
\(m(2m+1)=k^{2}/2+m\).  Because \(m>0\), (3.2) is false.  Hence **no even
\(k\ge2\) is possible**.

*Odd \(k\).*  Write \(k=2m+1\;(m\ge0)\).  Then \(\bigl\lfloor(k+1)/2\bigr\rfloor=m+1\)
and (3.2) becomes an equality:

\[
(2m+1)(m+1)=\frac{(2m+1)(2m+2)}2 .
\tag{3.3}
\]

Consequently every sunny line must contain **exactly** \(m+1\) points of
\(T_{2m+1}\), and the \(k\) lines must be pairwise disjoint.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  Sunny lines that attain the bound

Equation (2.1) with \(|p+q|=2\) gives three possibilities:

* \(p=q=1\) (slope \(1\));
* \(p=-2,\;q=1\) (slope \(-2\));
* \(p=-1,\;q=2\) (slope \(-\tfrac12\)).

For \(k=2m+1\) the corresponding lines are exactly the three lines listed in
(10).  A direct substitution shows that each of them contains \(m+1\) points of
\(T_{2m+1}\) and that the three point‑sets are disjoint.  No other sunny line
can contain \(m+1\) points, because any other choice would have \(|p+q|\ge3\)
or \(|p+q|=1\) with \(q\ge2\), and then (2.4) gives a strictly smaller
upper bound.

Thus, to cover \(T_{2m+1}\) with \(2m+1\) sunny lines we must use **only**
the three lines (10).  Hence we need \(2m+1\le3\); i.e. \(k=1\) or
\(k=3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.  Constructions for the admissible values

* **\(k=0\).**  
  The \(n\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n\) are all non‑sunny and cover
  every point of \(S_n\).

* **\(k=1\).**  
  Use the \(n-1\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n-1\).  
  The only uncovered point is \((n,1)\).  The sunny line  

  \[
  \ell:\; y=2x-2n+1
  \]

  passes through \((n,1)\) and is not parallel to any forbidden direction.
  Together the \(n\) lines satisfy the requirements.

* **\(k=3\).**  
  Use the \(n-3\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n-3\).  
  The uncovered set is \(T_3\).  The three sunny lines

  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  L_{1}&: y=x,\\
  L_{2}&: y=-2x+5,\\
  L_{3}&: y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac52
  \end{aligned}
  \]

  contain respectively the points  

  \[
  \begin{array}{l}
  L_{1}:\;(1,1),(2,2),\\[2pt]
  L_{2}:\;(1,3),(2,1),\\[2pt]
  L_{3}:\;(1,2),(3,1),
  \end{array}
  \]

  which are exactly the six points of \(T_3\).  Hence all points of
  \(S_n\) are covered.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.  Conclusion

The only non‑negative integers \(k\) for which a configuration of \(n\) distinct
lines (with exactly \(k\) sunny) covering all points \((a,b)\) with
\(a+b\le n+1\) exists are  

\[
\boxed{\;k\in\{0,1,3\}\;}
\]

for every integer \(n\ge3\).  The three families of constructions above show
that each of these values is indeed attainable.
